subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Show that the equation 2x²−13xy−7y²+x+23y−6=0 represents a pair of straight lines. Also find the angle between them and the coordinates of the point of intersection.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — name the four conditions, and say which quantity you can reuse for the angle.

steps.label: Compare the coefficients
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Every test that follows is written in a, h, b, g, f, c — so read all six off the given equation first, halving the ones the standard form doubles.
lines: (the xy, x and y coefficients in the standard form are 2h,

recall.must_convey: That all six coefficients are read off, halving those the standard form writes doubled.
accept: compare with the standard form and read off all six coefficients
two h is seven so h is seven over two
halve the coefficients that the standard form doubles
standard form tho compare chesi coefficients teesukovali
read off a h b g f and c

steps.why: The standard form writes the xy, x and y coefficients DOUBLED, so the numbers read straight off the question have to be halved to become h, g and f. Skipping that halving is a common error in this type of question.
common_mistakes: Taking h as the whole xy coefficient instead of half of it.
Getting the sign of a negative coefficient wrong.
steps.memory_tip: Read all six of a, h, b, g, f, c off first, HALVING the ones the standard form doubles.

steps.label: Test Δ = 0
steps.margin_note: First mark. Δ = abc + 2fgh − af² − bg² − ch² is the first test — it is zero exactly when the equation factors into two linear factors, which may not be real.

lines.text: (the first of the four conditions for a pair of lines is Δ = 0)

recall.must_convey: That Δ = abc + 2fgh − af² − bg² − ch² is computed and comes out zero.
accept: compute the determinant condition and show it is zero
delta is a b c plus two f g h minus a f squared minus b g squared minus c h squared
substituting gives zero
delta zero ani chupinchali
the master test is delta equals zero
heard_as: a b c plus two f g h

steps.why: Δ = 0 is necessary AND sufficient together with the inequalities — it is the standard condition for a general second-degree equation to represent a pair of lines.
common_mistakes: Dropping one of the five terms of Δ.
Arithmetic slip with the quarters that come from halved coefficients.
steps.memory_tip: Δ = abc + 2fgh − af² − bg² − ch² is zero exactly when the equation factors into two linear factors (real or not).

steps.label: Test the three inequalities
steps.margin_note: One mark. Δ = 0 alone is not enough — the three inequalities confirm the factors are REAL rather than complex. All four conditions together prove it.
lines: All the four conditions are satisfied.
So, the given equation represents a pair of straight lines.

recall.must_convey: That h² − ab, f² − bc and g² − ac are all computed and found non-negative.
accept: check h squared minus a b, f squared minus b c and g squared minus a c
all three must be greater than or equal to zero
these confirm the lines are real
moodu inequalities check cheyyali
all four conditions are satisfied

steps.why: Δ = 0 says the equation factors; the inequalities say it factors over the REALS. An equation can satisfy Δ = 0 and still describe no real lines at all.
common_mistakes: Stopping at Δ = 0 and declaring the answer.
Testing only one of the three inequalities.
steps.memory_tip: Δ = 0 alone is not enough — the three inequalities confirm the factors are REAL.
lines_compact: All the four conditions are satisfied.
So, the given equation represents a pair of straight lines.

steps.label: Find the point of intersection
steps.margin_note: One mark. The two lines meet at a point given directly by a formula in the same six coefficients — no factorising and no solving is needed.

lines.text: (the point of intersection of the pair of lines)

recall.must_convey: That the point of intersection is ((hf − bg)/(ab − h²), (gh − af)/(ab − h²)).
accept: the point of intersection is h f minus b g over a b minus h squared and g h minus a f over the same
use the point of intersection formula in the coefficients
no factorising is needed, the formula gives it directly
point of intersection formula vaadali
this gives the point

steps.why: Both coordinates share the denominator ab − h², which is non-zero precisely because the lines are not parallel — so the formula is safe exactly when the point exists.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two numerators between x and y.
Using ab + h² in the denominator.
steps.memory_tip: A formula in the same six coefficients gives the meeting point — no factorising, no solving.

steps.label: Find the angle between them
steps.margin_note: The last mark. The angle between the two lines of a pair comes from the same coefficients again — tanθ = 2√(h² − ab) / |a + b|, using the h² − ab already computed above.
lines: The angle between the pair is given by

recall.must_convey: That tanθ = 2√(h² − ab)/|a + b| = 3, so θ = Cos⁻¹(1/√10).
accept: tan theta is two root h squared minus a b over mod a plus b
tan theta comes out three so cos theta is one over root ten
reuse the h squared minus a b already found
tan theta formula vaadali
the angle is cos inverse one by root ten
heard_as: two root h squared minus a b

steps.why: h² − ab was already computed for the inequality test, so the angle needs almost no extra work.
common_mistakes: Writing h = −13 instead of −13/2 in h² − ab, which gives tanθ = 2√183/5 instead of 3.
Dropping the modulus on |a + b|: here a + b = −5, so a negative tangent comes out.
steps.memory_tip: tan θ = 2√(h² − ab)/|a + b|, reusing the h² − ab already computed.

insider_note: h, g and f are all halves here, so work over a denominator of 4 rather than decimalising. Four things are marked: Δ = 0, the three inequalities, the point of intersection, and the angle from tanθ = 2√(h² − ab)/|a + b|.
